question: What is a requirement of all marine transmitting apparatus used aboard United States vessels?
choices: Only equipment that has been certified by the FCC for Part 80 operations is authorized.
Equipment must be type-accepted by the U.S. Coast Guard for maritime mobile use.
Certification is required by the International Maritime Organization (IMO).
Programming of all maritime channels must be performed by a licensed Marine Radio Operator.
explanation: FCC Part 80 requires all marine transmitting equipment aboard U.S. vessels to be certified (type-accepted) specifically for Part 80 use - another agency's approval isn't enough on its own.

question: What transmitting equipment is authorized for use by a station in the maritime services?
choices: Transmitters that have been certified by the manufacturer for maritime use.
Unless specifically excepted, only transmitters certified by the Federal Communications Commission for Part 80 operations.
Equipment that has been inspected and approved by the U.S. Coast Guard.
Transceivers and transmitters that meet all ITU specifications for use in maritime mobile service.
explanation: Same Part 80 certification rule applied to equipment authorized for maritime use generally: FCC certification, not manufacturer self-certification or ITU specs alone, is what authorizes a maritime transmitter.

question: Small passenger vessels that sail 20 to 150 nautical miles from the nearest land must have what additional equipment?
choices: Inmarsat-B terminal.
Inmarsat-C terminal.
Aircraft Transceiver with 121.5 MHz.
MF-HF SSB Transceiver.
explanation: Beyond VHF's roughly 20-mile range, GMDSS Sea Area A2 coverage (20-150 nautical miles offshore) requires an MF-HF SSB transceiver.
choice_notes: Inmarsat-B: an older satellite terminal for voice/telex/data (large stabilized dish), not the coastal requirement.
Inmarsat-C: satellite store-and-forward messaging terminal (GMDSS A3), not what this rule requires.
121.5 MHz is the aeronautical emergency/homing frequency, for aircraft and beacon homing.

question: What equipment is programmed to initiate transmission of distress alerts and calls to individual stations?
choices: NAVTEX.
GPS.
DSC controller.
Scanning Watch Receiver.
explanation: Digital Selective Calling (DSC) is the GMDSS technology for automatically sending distress alerts and individual calls; the DSC controller is the equipment that generates them.
choice_notes: NAVTEX: a receive-only printer for MSI (warnings, weather) on 518 kHz. It can't transmit.
GPS: provides position to the DSC controller but transmits nothing.
Scanning watch receiver: only listens to the DSC frequencies. It can't send calls.

question: What is the minimum transmitter power level required by the FCC for a medium-frequency transmitter aboard a compulsorily fitted vessel?
choices: At least 100 watts, single-sideband, suppressed-carrier power.
At least 60 watts PEP.
The power predictably needed to communicate with the nearest public coast station operating on 2182 kHz.
At least 25 watts delivered into 50 ohms effective resistance when operated with a primary voltage of 13.6 volts DC.
explanation: Part 80 sets a 60-watt PEP minimum transmitter power for MF equipment on compulsorily fitted vessels, ensuring adequate distress/calling range.

question: Shipboard transmitters using F3E emission (FM voice) may not exceed what carrier power?
choices: 500 watts.
250 watts.
100 watts.
25 watts.
explanation: FCC rules cap shipboard VHF-FM (F3E) carrier power at 25 watts to limit interference while still covering normal VHF range.

question: Which commercial radio operator license is required to operate a fixed-tuned ship RADAR station with external controls?
choices: A radio operator certificate containing a Ship RADAR Endorsement.
A Marine Radio Operator Permit or higher.
Either a First or Second Class Radiotelegraph certificate or a General Radiotelephone Operator License.
No radio operator authorization is required.
explanation: A fixed-tuned RADAR with external controls needs no operator license because the operator adjusts only the display, not the transmitter's technical settings.

question: When is a Marine Radio Operator Permit or higher license required for aircraft communications?
choices: When operating on frequencies below 30 MHz allocated exclusively to aeronautical mobile services.
When operating on frequencies above 30 MHz allocated exclusively to aeronautical mobile services.
When operating on frequencies below 30 MHz not allocated exclusively to aeronautical mobile services.
When operating on frequencies above 30 MHz not assigned for international use.
explanation: Below 30 MHz, frequencies shared with other services (not allocated exclusively to aeronautical mobile) require at least a Marine Radio Operator Permit for aircraft communications.
choice_notes: Exclusively aeronautical frequencies are handled under aviation rules, not by this permit requirement.
Above 30 MHz (VHF) aeronautical operation needs no commercial operator licence in most cases.
No such licence trigger exists for frequencies above 30 MHz.

question: Which of the following persons are ineligible to be issued a commercial radio operator license?
choices: Individuals who are unable to send and receive correctly by telephone spoken messages in English.
Handicapped persons with uncorrected disabilities which affect their ability to perform all duties required of commercial radio operators.
Foreign maritime radio operators unless they are certified by the International Maritime Organization (IMO).
U.S. Military radio operators who are still on active duty.
explanation: FCC rules require commercial radio operators to communicate clearly by telephone in English; someone who can't do so cannot be issued the license.

question: What are the radio operator requirements of a passenger ship equipped with a GMDSS installation?
choices: The operator must hold a General Radiotelephone Operator License or higher-class license.
The operator must hold a Restricted Radiotelephone Operator Permit or higher-class license.
The operator must hold a Marine Radio Operator Permit or higher-class license.
Two operators on board must hold a GMDSS Radio Operator License or a Restricted GMDSS Radio Operator License, depending on the ship’s operating areas.
explanation: A GMDSS-equipped passenger ship must carry two qualified radio operators, each holding either the full GMDSS Radio Operator License or the Restricted version appropriate to the ship's operating areas.

question: What is the minimum radio operator requirement for ships subject to the Great Lakes Radio Agreement?
choices: Third Class Radiotelegraph Operator’s Certificate.
General Radiotelephone Operator License.
Marine Radio Operator Permit.
Restricted Radiotelephone Operator Permit.
explanation: Ships subject to the Great Lakes Radio Agreement need at least a Marine Radio Operator Permit to operate the station.

question: What is a requirement of every commercial operator on duty and in charge of a transmitting system?
choices: A copy of the Proof-of-Passing Certificate (PPC) must be in the station’s records.
The original license or a photocopy must be posted or in the operator’s personal possession and available for inspection.
The FCC Form 605 certifying the operator’s qualifications must be readily available at the transmitting system site.
A copy of the operator’s license must be supplied to the radio station’s supervisor as evidence of technical qualification.
explanation: The commercial operator on duty must have the original license, or a photocopy, posted at the station or kept on their person and available for FCC inspection.

question: Radio watches for compulsory radiotelephone stations will include the following:
choices: VHF channel 22a continuous watch at sea.
121.5 MHz continuous watch at sea.
VHF channel 16 continuous watch.
500 kHz.
explanation: Compulsory radiotelephone stations keep a continuous watch on VHF Channel 16, the international calling and distress channel.
choice_notes: Ch-22A is the US Coast Guard liaison/working channel, not a mandatory watch.
121.5 MHz is the aeronautical emergency frequency, used for aircraft and beacon homing.
500 kHz was the old Morse (radiotelegraph) distress frequency, retired with GMDSS.

question: All compulsory equipped cargo ships (except those operating under GMDSS regulations or in a VTS) while being navigated outside of a harbor or port, shall keep a continuous radiotelephone watch on:
choices: 2182 kHz and Ch-16.
Cargo ships are exempt from radio watch regulations.
explanation: Non-GMDSS compulsory cargo ships, while navigating outside a harbor/VTS, must watch both the MF distress/calling frequency 2182 kHz and VHF Channel 16.

question: What channel must all compulsory, non-GMDSS vessels monitor at all times in the open sea?
choices: Channel 8.
Channel 70.
Channel 6.
Channel 16.
explanation: VHF Channel 16 is the universal distress/calling channel that non-GMDSS vessels must monitor continuously while at sea.
choice_notes: Ch-8: intership working channel for commercial vessels.
Ch-70: reserved for DSC data only, which you can't listen to.
Ch-6: intership safety channel (e.g. SAR coordination with aircraft).

question: When a watch is required on 2182 kHz, at how many minutes past the hour must a 3 minute silent period be observed?
explanation: The mandatory 3-minute silent periods on 2182 kHz fall at :00 and :30 past each hour, so weak distress signals can be heard.

question: Which is true concerning a required watch on VHF Ch-16?
choices: It is compulsory at all times while at sea until further notice, unless the vessel is in a VTS system.
When a vessel is in an A1 sea area and subject to the Bridge-to-Bridge act and in a VTS system, a watch is not required on Ch-16, provided the vessel monitors both Ch-13 and VTS channel.
It is always compulsory in sea areas A2, A3 and A4.
All of the above.
explanation: All three statements about the required VHF Ch-16 watch - continuous at sea, with the specific VTS exception when monitoring Ch-13 and the VTS channel instead - are correct together.

question: What are the mandatory DSC watchkeeping bands/channels?
choices: VHF Ch-70, 2 MHz MF DSC, 6 MHz DSC and 1 other HF DSC.
8 MHz HF DSC, 1 other HF DSC, 2 MHz MF DSC and VHF Ch-70.
2 MHz MF DSC, 8 MHz DSC, VHF Ch-16 and 1 other HF DSC.
None of the above.
explanation: GMDSS requires simultaneous DSC watchkeeping on VHF Ch-70, 2 MHz MF DSC, and 8 MHz plus one other HF DSC band suited to the ship's sea area.
choice_notes: 6 MHz DSC can be the 'other' HF channel, but the mandatory one is 8 MHz.
Ch-16 is a voice channel. The VHF DSC watch is on Ch-70.

question: Who is required to make entries in a required service or maintenance log?
choices: The licensed operator or a person whom he or she designates.
The operator responsible for the station operation or maintenance.
Any commercial radio operator holding at least a Restricted Radiotelephone Operator Permit.
The technician who actually makes the adjustments to the equipment.
explanation: Whoever is responsible for operating or maintaining the station is the one required to make the corresponding service/maintenance log entries.

question: Who is responsible for the proper maintenance of station logs?
choices: The station licensee.
The commercially-licensed radio operator in charge of the station.
The ship’s master and the station licensee.
The station licensee and the radio operator in charge of the station.
explanation: Responsibility for proper log maintenance is shared between the station licensee and the radio operator in charge of the station.

question: Where must ship station logs be kept during a voyage?
choices: At the principal radiotelephone operating position.
They must be secured in the vessel’s strongbox for safekeeping.
In the personal custody of the licensed commercial radio operator.
All logs are turned over to the ship’s master when the radio operator goes off duty.
explanation: Station logs must be kept at the principal radiotelephone operating position, where the radio is actually used, so they're always available.

question: What is the proper procedure for making a correction in the station log?
choices: The ship’s master must be notified, approve and initial all changes to the station log.
The mistake may be erased and the correction made and initialized only by the radio operator making the original error.
The original person making the entry must strike out the error, initial the correction and indicate the date of the correction.
Rewrite the new entry in its entirety directly below the incorrect notation and initial the change.
explanation: A log correction is made by striking through the error (never erasing it), then the original entrant initials and dates the correction, preserving the original record.

question: How long should station logs be retained when there are entries relating to distress or disaster situations?
choices: Until authorized by the Commission in writing to destroy them.
For a period of three years from the last date of entry, unless notified by the FCC.
Indefinitely, or until destruction is specifically authorized by the U.S. Coast Guard.
For a period of one year from the last date of entry.
explanation: Logs containing distress/disaster entries must be kept for 3 years from the last entry date, unless the FCC directs otherwise - longer than ordinary logs.

question: How long should station logs be retained when there are no entries relating to distress or disaster situations?
choices: For a period of three years from the last date of entry, unless notified by the FCC.
Until authorized by the Commission in writing to destroy them.
For a period of two years from the last date of entry.
Indefinitely, or until destruction is specifically authorized by the U.S. Coast Guard.
explanation: Without any distress/disaster entries, the retention period is shorter: 2 years from the last date of entry.

question: Radiotelephone stations required to keep logs of their transmissions must include:
choices: Station, date and time.
Name of operator on duty.
Station call signs with which communication took place.
All of these.
explanation: A transmission log entry must record all of these together - the station, the date and time, the operator on duty, and the call signs worked.

question: Which of the following is true?
choices: Battery test must be logged daily.
EPIRB tests are normally logged monthly.
Radiotelephone tests are normally logged weekly.
None of the above.
explanation: EPIRB tests are a monthly requirement, distinct from the more frequent daily checks of other GMDSS equipment.

question: Where should the GMDSS radio log be kept on board ship?
choices: Captain’s office.
Sea cabin.
At the GMDSS operating position.
Anywhere on board the vessel.
explanation: Like the general station log, the GMDSS radio log must be kept right at the GMDSS operating position.

question: Which of the following statements is true?
choices: Key letters or abbreviations may be used in GMDSS Radio Logbooks if their meaning is noted in the log.
Key letters or abbreviations may not be used in GMDSS Radio Logbooks under any circumstances.
All Urgency communications must be entered in the logbook.
None of the above.
explanation: Abbreviations are permitted in a GMDSS log as long as their meaning is noted somewhere in the log, keeping the record unambiguous.

question: Which of the following logkeeping statements is true?
choices: Entries relating to pre-voyage, pre-departure and daily tests are required.
Both a) and c)

A summary of all required Distress communications heard and Urgency communications affecting the station’s own ship. Also, all Safety communications (other than VHF) affecting the station’s own ship must be logged.
Routine daily MF-HF and Inmarsat-C transmissions do not have to be logged.
explanation: Both the pre-voyage/pre-departure/daily test entries and the required summary of Distress/Urgency communications and other Safety traffic are genuine logkeeping requirements.

question: Which of the following statements concerning log entries is false?
choices: All Safety communications received on VHF must be logged.
All required equipment tests must be logged.
The radio operator must log on and off watch.
The vessels daily position must be entered in the log.
explanation: This is the false statement: not every Safety call received on VHF needs a full log entry - only Distress/Urgency traffic and designated Safety broadcasts do, unlike the other three choices, which are accurate requirements.

question: What regulations govern the use and operation of FCC-licensed ship stations in international waters?
choices: The regulations of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and Radio Officers Union.
Part 80 of the FCC Rules plus the international Radio Regulations and agreements to which the United States is a party.
The Maritime Mobile Directives of the International Telecommunication Union.
Those of the FCC’s Wireless Telecommunications Bureau, Maritime Mobile Service, Washington, DC 20554.
explanation: Ship stations are governed both by FCC Part 80 domestically and by the ITU Radio Regulations and related international agreements when operating in international waters.

question: When may the operator of a ship radio station allow an unlicensed person to speak over the transmitter?
choices: At no time. Only commercially-licensed radio operators may modulate the transmitting apparatus.
When the station power does not exceed 200 watts peak envelope power.
When under the supervision of the licensed operator.
During the hours that the radio officer is normally off duty.
explanation: An unlicensed person may use the transmitter only under the direct supervision of a licensed operator, who remains responsible for proper operation.

question: Where do you make an application for inspection of a ship GMDSS radio station?
choices: To a Commercial Operator Licensing Examination Manager (COLE Manager).
To the Federal Communications Commission, Washington, DC 20554.
To the Engineer-in-Charge of the FCC District Office nearest the proposed place of inspection.
To an FCC-licensed technician holding a GMDSS Radio Maintainer’s License.
explanation: Inspection requests for a ship GMDSS station go to the Engineer-in-Charge of the FCC District Office nearest where the inspection will take place.

question: Who has ultimate control of service at a ship’s radio station?
choices: The master of the ship.
A holder of a First Class Radiotelegraph Certificate with a six months’ service endorsement.
The Radio Officer-in-Charge authorized by the captain of the vessel.
An appointed licensed radio operator who agrees to comply with all Radio Regulations in force.
explanation: The ship's master holds ultimate authority over the radio station's service, even though a licensed operator runs the equipment day to day.

question: Where must the principal radiotelephone operating position be installed in a ship station?
choices: At the principal radio operating position of the vessel.
In the chart room, master’s quarters or wheel house.
In the room or an adjoining room from which the ship is normally steered while at sea.
At the level of the main wheel house or at least one deck above the ship’s main deck.
explanation: The principal radiotelephone operating position must be in, or adjoining, the room from which the ship is normally steered at sea, so it's quickly reachable.

question: By international agreement, which ships must carry radio equipment for the safety of life at sea?
choices: All ships traveling more than 100 miles out to sea.
Cargo ships of more than 100 gross tons and passenger vessels on international deep-sea voyages.
All cargo ships of more than 100 gross tons.
Cargo ships of more than 300 gross tons and vessels carrying more than 12 passengers.
explanation: SOLAS sets these as the thresholds for mandatory life-safety radio equipment: cargo ships over 300 gross tons, and any vessel carrying more than 12 passengers.

question: What traffic management service is operated by the U.S. Coast Guard in certain designated water areas to prevent ship collisions, groundings and environmental harm?
choices: Water Safety Management Bureau (WSMB).
Vessel Traffic Service (VTS).
Ship Movement and Safety Agency (SMSA).
Interdepartmental Harbor and Port Patrol (IHPP).
explanation: The Coast Guard's Vessel Traffic Service manages ship movements in designated high-traffic or hazardous waterways to prevent collisions, groundings, and environmental harm.
choice_notes: Invented name, no such service.
Invented name, no such agency.
Invented name, no such patrol.

question: What is a bridge-to-bridge station?
choices: An internal communications system linking the wheel house with the ship’s primary radio operating position and other integral ship control points.
An inland waterways and coastal radio station serving ship stations operating within the United States.
A portable ship station necessary to eliminate frequent application to operate a ship station on board different vessels.
A VHF radio station located on a ship’s navigational bridge or main control station that is used only for navigational communications.
explanation: A bridge-to-bridge station is a VHF radio on the ship's navigational bridge used strictly for navigational safety communications between vessels, not general traffic.
choice_notes: That describes an internal ship communication system (intercom/sound-powered phones).
That describes a public or limited coast station.
That describes a portable ship station licence.

question: When may a bridge-to-bridge transmission be more than 1 watt?
choices: When broadcasting a distress message and rounding a bend in a river or traveling in a blind spot.
When broadcasting a distress message.
When rounding a bend in a river or traveling in a blind spot.
When calling the Coast Guard.
explanation: Channel 13 bridge-to-bridge power is normally limited to 1 watt, but higher power is allowed when needed for safety - such as sending a distress message or getting the signal around a bend or blind spot.

question: When is it legal to transmit high power on Channel 13?
choices: Failure of vessel being called to respond.
In a blind situation such as rounding a bend in a river.
During an emergency.
All of these.
explanation: All three listed situations - failure of the called vessel to respond, a blind spot or bend in the river, and an emergency - justify switching to high power on Channel 13.

question: A ship station using VHF bridge-to-bridge Channel 13:
choices: May be identified by the name of the ship in lieu of call sign.
May be identified by call sign and country of origin.
Must be identified by call sign and name of vessel.
Does not need to identify itself within 100 miles from shore.
explanation: On bridge-to-bridge Channel 13, a vessel may identify itself by name instead of its FCC call sign, since the channel's purpose is immediate navigational safety, not formal identification.

question: The primary purpose of bridge-to-bridge communications is:
choices: Search and rescue emergency calls only.
All short-range transmission aboard ship.
Navigational communications.
Transmission of Captain's orders from the bridge.
explanation: Bridge-to-bridge communications exist primarily to coordinate safe passing and navigation between vessels, not for general ship's business.

question: What is the best way for a radio operator to minimize or prevent interference to other stations?
choices: By using an omni-directional antenna pointed away from other stations.
Reducing power to a level that will not affect other on-frequency communications.
Determine that a frequency is not in use by monitoring the frequency before transmitting.
By changing frequency when notified that a radiocommunication causes interference.
explanation: Listening to confirm a frequency is clear before transmitting is the basic way any operator avoids interfering with ongoing communications.

question: Under what circumstances may a coast station using telephony transmit a general call to a group of vessels?
choices: Under no circumstances.
When announcing or preceding the transmission of Distress, Urgency, Safety or other important messages.
When the vessels are located in international waters beyond 12 miles.
When identical traffic is destined for multiple mobile stations within range.
explanation: A coast station may call a group of vessels specifically to announce or introduce high-priority traffic - a Distress, Urgency, Safety, or other important message.

question: Who determines when a ship station may transmit routine traffic destined for a coast or government station in the maritime mobile service?
choices: Shipboard radio officers may transmit traffic when it will not interfere with ongoing radiocommunications.
The order and time of transmission and permissible type of message traffic is decided by the licensed on- duty operator.
Ship stations must comply with instructions given by the coast or government station.
The precedence of conventional radiocommunications is determined by FCC and international regulation.
explanation: The coast or government station controls the timing of routine ship traffic directed to it, and ship stations must comply with its instructions.

question: What is required of a ship station which has established initial contact with another station on 2182 kHz or Ch-16?
choices: The stations must change to an authorized working frequency for the transmission of messages.
The stations must check the radio channel for Distress, Urgency and Safety calls at least once every ten minutes.
Radiated power must be minimized so as not to interfere with other stations needing to use the channel.
To expedite safety communications, the vessels must observe radio silence for two out of every fifteen minutes.
explanation: 2182 kHz and Channel 16 are reserved for calling and distress only - once contact is made, both stations must shift to an authorized working frequency to continue.

question: How does a coast station notify a ship that it has a message for the ship?
choices: By making a directed transmission on 2182 kHz or 156.800 MHz.
The coast station changes to the vessel’s known working frequency.
By establishing communications using the eight-digit maritime mobile service identification.
The coast station may transmit, at intervals, lists of call signs in alphabetical order for which they have traffic.
explanation: A coast station periodically broadcasts an alphabetical list of call signs it is holding traffic for, so ships know to check in and collect their messages.

question: What is the priority of communications?
choices: Safety, Distress, Urgency and radio direction-finding.
Distress, Urgency and Safety.
Distress, Safety, radio direction-finding, search and rescue.
Radio direction-finding, Distress and Safety.
explanation: The universal maritime priority order, highest first, is Distress, then Urgency, then Safety.
choice_notes: Safety ranks below Distress and Urgency. RDF isn't a priority category in this order.
Mixes in RDF and SAR, which aren't priority levels. Urgency is missing.
RDF isn't a priority category, and Urgency is missing.

question: Under what circumstances may a ship or aircraft station interfere with a public coast station?
choices: In cases of distress.
Under no circumstances during on-going radiocommunications.
During periods of government priority traffic handling.
When it is necessary to transmit a message concerning the safety of navigation or important meteorological warnings.
explanation: Distress overrides all other considerations, including the normal rule against interfering with a public coast station's transmissions.

question: Ordinarily, how often would a station using a telephony emission identify?
choices: At least every 10 minutes.
At the beginning and end of each transmission and at 15-minute intervals.
At 15-minute intervals, unless public correspondence is in progress.
At 20-minute intervals.
explanation: A telephony station must identify at the start and end of a transmission, and at 15-minute intervals during a longer exchange.

question: When using a SSB station on 2182 kHz or VHF-FM on channel 16:
choices: Preliminary call must not exceed 30 seconds.
If contact is not made, you must wait at least 2 minutes before repeating the call.
Once contact is established, you must switch to a working frequency.
All of these.
explanation: All the listed practices for making initial contact on 2182 kHz/Channel 16 - monitoring first, keeping the call brief, and shifting to a working frequency - apply together.

question: What should a station operator do before making a transmission?
choices: Except for the transmission of distress calls, determine that the frequency is not in use by monitoring the frequency before transmitting.
Transmit a general notification that the operator wishes to utilize the channel.
Check transmitting equipment to be certain it is properly calibrated.
Ask if the frequency is in use.
explanation: Except when sending a distress call, an operator must confirm a frequency is clear by monitoring it before transmitting.

question: On what frequency should a ship station normally call a coast station when using a radiotelephony emission?
choices: On a vacant radio channel determined by the licensed radio officer.
Calls should be initiated on the appropriate ship-to-shore working frequency of the coast station.
On any calling frequency internationally approved for use within ITU Region 2.
On 2182 kHz or Ch-16 at any time.
explanation: A routine call to a coast station should be made directly on its published ship-to-shore working frequency, not on the calling/distress channel.

question: In the International Phonetic Alphabet, the letters E, M, and S are represented by the words:
choices: Echo, Michigan, Sonar.
Equator, Mike, Sonar.
Echo, Mike, Sierra
Element, Mister, Scooter
explanation: Echo, Mike, and Sierra are the standard ITU phonetic alphabet words for the letters E, M, and S.
choice_notes: Michigan and Sonar aren't ICAO/ITU phonetic words.
Equator and Sonar aren't phonetic words.
None of these are phonetic alphabet words.

question: What information must be included in a Distress message?
choices: Name of vessel.
Location.
Type of distress and specifics of help requested.
All of the above.
explanation: A complete distress message needs everything listed - identification, position, the nature of the distress, and the assistance required - so rescuers can respond effectively.

question: What are the highest priority communications from ships at sea?
choices: All critical message traffic authorized by the ship’s master.
Navigation and meteorological warnings.
Distress calls are highest and then communications preceded by Urgency and then Safety signals.
Authorized government communications for which priority right has been claimed.
explanation: This restates the standard priority order: Distress calls rank highest, followed by traffic preceded by Urgency, then Safety signals.

question: What is a Distress communication?
choices: Communications indicating that the calling station has a very urgent message concerning safety.
An internationally recognized communication indicating that the sender is threatened by grave and imminent danger and requests immediate assistance.
Radio communications which, if delayed, will adversely affect the safety of life or property.
An official radio communication notification of approaching navigational or meteorological hazards.
explanation: This is the formal definition of a Distress communication under international radio regulations: grave and imminent danger, with a request for immediate assistance.
choice_notes: That describes Urgency (PAN PAN).
This is close to the Urgency/Safety definition, not grave and imminent danger.
That describes a Safety message (SECURITE).

question: What is the order of priority of radiotelephone communications in the maritime services?
choices: Alarm and health and welfare communications.
Navigation hazards, meteorological warnings, priority traffic.
Distress calls and signals, followed by communications preceded by Urgency and Safety signals and all other communications.
Government precedence, messages concerning safety of life and protection of property, and traffic concerning grave and imminent danger.
explanation: This lays out the complete priority chain: Distress calls and signals first, then traffic preceded by Urgency and Safety signals, then all other communications.

question: The radiotelephone Distress call and message consists of:
choices: MAYDAY spoken three times, followed by the name of the vessel and the call sign in phonetics spoken three times.
Particulars of its position, latitude and longitude, and other information which might facilitate rescue, such as length, color and type of vessel, and number of persons on board.
Nature of distress and kind of assistance required.
All of the above.
explanation: The full distress call and message together include all the listed elements - the distress signal, identification, position, and details of the emergency.

question: What is Distress traffic?
choices: All messages relative to the immediate assistance required by a ship, aircraft or other vehicle threatened by grave or imminent danger, such as life and safety of persons on board, or man overboard.
In radiotelephony, the speaking of the word, “Mayday.”
Health and welfare messages concerning property and the safety of a vessel.
Internationally recognized communications relating to important situations.
explanation: Distress traffic covers all messages directly related to the immediate assistance needed by a ship, aircraft, or person facing grave or imminent danger.

question: What is a typical Urgency transmission?
choices: A request for medical assistance that does not rise to the level of a Distress or a critical weather transmission higher than Safety.
A radio Distress transmission affecting the security of humans or property.
Health and welfare traffic which impacts the protection of on-board personnel.
A communications alert that important personal messages must be transmitted.
explanation: Urgency traffic covers situations serious but not immediately life-threatening, such as a non-critical medical request or a weather warning more pressing than ordinary Safety traffic.
choice_notes: That would be Distress (MAYDAY).
Routine health and welfare traffic has no priority signal.

question: What is the internationally recognized Urgency signal?
choices: The letters “TTT” transmitted three times by radiotelegraphy.
The words “PAN PAN” spoken three times before the Urgency call.
Three oral repetitions of the word “Safety” sent before the call.
The pronouncement of the word “Mayday.”
explanation: PAN PAN, spoken three times, is the internationally recognized spoken Urgency signal, one priority level below MAYDAY.
choice_notes: TTT was the old radiotelegraph Safety signal.
The voice Safety signal is SECURITE, not the word 'Safety'.
MAYDAY is the Distress signal.

question: What is a Safety transmission?
choices: A communications transmission which indicates that a station is preparing to transmit an important navigation or weather warning.
A radiotelephony warning preceded by the words “PAN PAN.”
Health and welfare traffic concerning the protection of human life.
A voice call proceeded by the words “Safety Alert.”
explanation: A Safety transmission is the announcement that an important navigational or meteorological warning is about to follow.
choice_notes: PAN PAN introduces Urgency, not Safety.
Health and welfare traffic has no special signal.
The Safety call is SECURITE x3, not 'Safety Alert'.

question: The Urgency signal concerning the safety of a ship, aircraft or person shall be sent only on the authority of:
choices: Master of ship.
Person responsible for mobile station.
Either Master of ship or person responsible for mobile station.
An FCC-licensed operator.
explanation: Only the ship's master, or the person responsible for the mobile station, may authorize sending an Urgency signal.

question: The Urgency signal has lower priority than:
choices: Ship-to-ship routine calls.
Distress.
Safety.
Security.
explanation: In the priority hierarchy, Urgency ranks just below Distress - serious, but not the highest level of emergency.

question: What safety signal call word is spoken three times, followed by the station call letters spoken three times, to announce a storm warning, danger to navigation, or special aid to navigation?
choices: PAN PAN.
MAYDAY.
SAFETY.
SECURITE.
explanation: SECURITE, spoken three times, is the international spoken Safety signal that precedes navigation or weather warnings.
choice_notes: PAN PAN = Urgency (safety of a ship or person).
MAYDAY = Distress (grave and imminent danger).
'Safety' isn't the spoken signal word. SECURITE is.

question: What is the fundamental concept of the GMDSS?
choices: It is intended to automate and improve existing digital selective calling procedures and techniques.
It is intended to provide more effective but lower cost commercial communications.
It is intended to provide compulsory vessels with a collision avoidance system when they are operating in waters that are also occupied by non-compulsory vessels.
It is intended to automate and improve emergency communications in the maritime industry.
explanation: GMDSS was designed to automate distress alerting and coordination, so emergencies no longer depend on a single operator manually sending a call.

question: The primary purpose of the GMDSS is to:
choices: Allow more effective control of SAR situations by vessels.
Provide additional shipboard systems for more effective company communications.
Automate and improve emergency communications for the world’s shipping industry.
Provide effective and inexpensive communications.
explanation: This restates GMDSS's core purpose: a worldwide, largely automated system for emergency communications across the shipping industry.

question: What is the basic concept of GMDSS?
choices: Shoreside authorities and vessels can assist in a coordinated SAR operation with minimum delay.
Search and rescue authorities ashore can be alerted to a Distress situation.
Shipping in the immediate vicinity of a ship in Distress will be rapidly alerted.
All of these.
explanation: All the listed concepts together make up the basic GMDSS design: automatic alerting, multiple independent communication paths, and coordination with search and rescue authorities.

question: GMDSS is primarily a system based on?
choices: Ship-to-ship Distress communications using MF or HF radiotelephony.
VHF digital selective calling from ship to shore.
Distress, Urgency and Safety communications carried out by the use of narrow-band direct printing telegraphy.
The linking of search and rescue authorities ashore with shipping in the immediate vicinity of a ship in Distress or in need of assistance.
explanation: GMDSS's core mechanism is linking shore-based search and rescue authorities with other vessels near a ship in distress, so help can be coordinated quickly.

question: What is the responsibility of vessels under GMDSS?
choices: Vessels over 300 gross tons may be required to render assistance if such assistance does not adversely affect their port schedule.
Only that vessel, regardless of size, closest to a vessel in Distress, is required to render assistance.
Every ship is able to perform those communications functions that are essential for the Safety of the ship itself and of other ships.
Vessels operating under GMDSS, outside of areas effectively serviced by shoreside authorities, operating in sea areas A2, and A4 may be required to render assistance in Distress situations.
explanation: Under GMDSS, every ship is responsible for having the communication capability needed to protect both itself and other ships nearby.

question: GMDSS is required for which of the following?
choices: All vessels capable of international voyages.
SOLAS Convention ships of 300 gross tonnage or more.
Vessels operating outside of the range of VHF coastal radio stations.
Coastal vessels of less than 300 gross tons.
explanation: GMDSS carriage requirements apply to SOLAS Convention ships of 300 gross tons or more on international voyages.

question: What is the purpose of the INT-USA control settings on a VHF?
choices: To change all VTS frequencies to Duplex so all vessels can receive maneuvering orders.
To change all VHF channels from Duplex to Simplex while in U.S. waters.
To change certain International Duplex channel assignments to simplex in the U.S. for VTS and other purposes.
To change to NOAA weather channels and receive weather broadcasts while in the U.S.
explanation: The INT/USA control reconfigures certain international duplex (repeater) channel assignments to simplex operation for U.S. uses such as VTS.

question: VHF ship station transmitters must have the capability of reducing carrier power to:
choices: 1 watt.
10 watts.
25 watts.
50 watts.
explanation: VHF ship transmitters must be able to step down to a low-power 1-watt setting for short-range or less critical communications.

question: The Dual Watch (DW) function is used to:
choices: Listen to Ch-70 at the same time while monitoring Ch-16.
Sequentially monitor 4 different channels.
Sequentially monitoring all VHF channels.
Listen on any selected channel while periodically monitoring Ch-16.
explanation: Dual Watch lets the operator stay on a chosen working channel while the radio automatically samples Channel 16 periodically, so a distress call isn't missed.
choice_notes: Ch-70 carries DSC data and is watched by the DSC receiver, not by ear.
That describes a priority/memory scan, not dual watch.
That describes the Scan function.

question: Which of the following statements best describes the correct setting for manual adjustment of the squelch control?
choices: Adjust squelch control to the minimum level necessary to barely suppress any background noise.
Always adjust squelch control to its maximum level.
Always adjust squelch control to its minimum level.
Adjust squelch control to approximately twice the minimum level necessary to barely suppress any background noise.
explanation: Proper squelch adjustment is the lowest threshold that still just suppresses background noise - set too high, you risk missing weak legitimate signals.

question: The “Scan” function is used to:
choices: Monitor Ch-16 continuously and switching to either Ch-70 or Ch-13 every 5 seconds.
Scan Ch-16 for Distress calls.
Scan Ch-70 for Distress alerts.
Sequentially scan all or selected channels.
explanation: The Scan function automatically steps through all channels, or a selected subset, listening briefly on each one for activity.
choice_notes: This combination isn't a standard function.
Watching Ch-16 is done by dual watch (or the radio's Ch-16 priority), not by Scan.
Ch-70 is watched by the DSC receiver, not scanned by voice.

question: Why must all VHF Distress, Urgency and Safety communications (as well as VTS traffic calls) be performed in Simplex operating mode?
choices: To minimize interference from vessels engaged in routine communications.
To ensure that vessels not directly participating in the communications can hear both sides of the radio exchange.
To enable an RCC or Coast station to only hear communications from the vessel actually in distress.
To allow an RCC or Coast station to determine which transmissions are from other vessels and which transmissions are from the vessel actually in distress.
explanation: Simplex keeps a whole exchange audible to everyone nearby on that frequency, which matters for Distress, Urgency, Safety, and VTS traffic that everyone should be able to follow.

question: What channel must VHF-FM-equipped vessels monitor at all times when the vessel is at sea?
choices: Channel 8.
Channel 16.
Channel 5A.
Channel 1A.
explanation: VHF Channel 16 remains the mandatory distress/calling channel that VHF-FM-equipped vessels must watch continuously while at sea.
choice_notes: Ch-8: intership working channel.
Ch-5A: VTS channel in some US ports (e.g. Seattle).
Ch-1A: VTS/port operations channel in some US areas.

question: What is the aircraft frequency and emission used for distress communications?
explanation: 121.5 MHz using A3E (amplitude-modulated voice) is the internationally designated aeronautical emergency frequency and emission type.
choice_notes: 243 MHz is the military aircraft emergency frequency, and it uses AM, not FM.
121.5 MHz is right, but aviation uses AM (A3E), not FM.
156.525 MHz is marine Ch-70 (DSC), not an aircraft frequency.

question: Which VHF channel is used only for digital selective calling?
choices: Channel 70.
Channel 16.
Channel 22A.
Channel 6.
explanation: VHF Channel 70 is reserved exclusively for Digital Selective Calling - no voice traffic is permitted there.
choice_notes: Ch-16: voice distress, safety and calling.
Ch-22A: US Coast Guard liaison/working channel (voice).
Ch-6: intership safety voice channel.

question: Which channel is utilized for the required bridge-to-bridge watch?
choices: DSC on Ch-70.
VHF-FM on Ch-16.
VHF-FM on Ch-13 in most areas of the continental United States.
The vessel’s VHF working frequency.
explanation: Channel 13 is designated for the mandatory bridge-to-bridge navigational watch throughout most of the continental United States.
choice_notes: Ch-70 is DSC only, not voice.
Ch-16 is distress/calling, not the bridge-to-bridge navigation channel.
A working channel isn't the required bridge-to-bridge watch.

question: Which channel would most likely be used for routine ship-to-ship voice traffic?
choices: Ch-22A.
explanation: Channel 8 is commonly used for routine ship-to-ship voice communications, separate from the calling/distress and bridge-to-bridge channels.
choice_notes: Ch-16 is for distress, safety and calling only, not traffic.
Ch-70 is DSC only.
Ch-22A is the Coast Guard liaison channel.

question: What channel would you use to place a call to a shore telephone?
explanation: Channel 28 is one of the public correspondence channels used to place a call to a shore telephone through a marine operator.
choice_notes: Ch-16: distress/calling, not phone calls.
Ch-70: DSC only.
Ch-6: intership safety.

question: Which modes could be selected to receive vessel traffic lists from high seas shore stations?
choices: AM and VHF-FM.
ARQ and FEC.
VHF-FM and SSB.
SSB and FEC.
explanation: High-seas coast stations broadcast their traffic lists using SSB voice and FEC (forward error correction) telex, both of which a vessel can receive to check for waiting messages.
choice_notes: AM isn't used by high-seas stations, and VHF-FM doesn't reach the high seas.
ARQ is two-way telex. Traffic lists are broadcast (FEC), not ARQ.
VHF-FM has too short a range for high-seas stations.

question: Why must all MF-HF Distress, Urgency and Safety communications take place solely on the 6 assigned frequencies and in the simplex operating mode?
choices: For non-GMDSS ships, to maximize the chances for other vessels to receive those communications.
Answers a) and c) are both correct.
For GMDSS or DSC-equipped ships, to maximize the chances for other vessels to receive those communications following the transmission of a DSC call of the correct priority.
To enable an RCC or Coast station to only hear communications from the vessel actually in distress.
explanation: Both reasons apply together: keeping everyone on a known, limited set of frequencies in simplex mode ensures Distress, Urgency, and Safety traffic is heard by every vessel monitoring, without duplex splitting the audience.

question: To set-up the MF/HF transceiver for a voice call to a coast station, the operator must:
choices: Select J3E mode for proper SITOR operations.
Select F1B mode or J2B mode, depending on the equipment manufacturer.
Select J3E mode for proper voice operations.
Select F1B/J2B modes or J3E mode, depending on whether FEC or ARQ is preferred.
explanation: J3E (single-sideband voice) is the correct emission mode to select before making a voice call to a coast station on MF/HF.
choice_notes: J3E is voice. SITOR needs F1B/J2B.
F1B/J2B are for telex (SITOR), not voice.
FEC and ARQ are telex modes and don't use J3E.

question: MF/HF transceiver power levels should be set:
choices: To the lowest level necessary for effective communications.
To the level necessary to maximize the propagation radius.
To the highest level possible so as to ensure other stations cannot “break-in” on the channel during use.
Both a) and c) are correct.
explanation: Good operating practice, and FCC rules, call for using only as much transmitter power as needed for reliable communication, not maximum power by default.

question: To set-up the MF/HF transceiver for a TELEX call to a coast station, the operator must:
choices: Select J3E mode for proper SITOR operations.
Select F1B mode or J2B mode, depending on the equipment manufacturer.
Select F1B/J2B modes or J3E mode, depending on whether ARQ or FEC is preferred.
None of the above.
explanation: A TELEX (NBDP) call uses a narrow-band direct-printing mode - F1B or J2B, depending on the radio's design - rather than a voice mode.
choice_notes: J3E is voice, not SITOR.
ARQ and FEC both use F1B/J2B. J3E is voice.

question: What is the purpose of the Receiver Incremental Tuning (RIT) or “Clarifier” control?
choices: It acts as a “fine-tune” control on the receive frequency.
It acts as a “fine-tune” control on the transmitted frequency.
It acts as a “fine-tune” control on both the receive and transmitted frequencies.
None of the above.
explanation: The Receiver Incremental Tuning (Clarifier) control makes small receive-only frequency adjustments to compensate for drift, without shifting the transmit frequency.
choice_notes: Fine-tuning the transmit frequency is XIT, not RIT.
Moving both together is just normal tuning, not the clarifier.

question: On what frequency would a vessel normally call another ship station when using a radiotelephony emission?
choices: Only on 2182 kHz in ITU Region 2.
On 2182 kHz or Ch-16, unless the station knows that the called vessel maintains a simultaneous watch on another intership working frequency.
On the appropriate calling channel of the ship station at 15 minutes past the hour.
On the vessel’s unique working radio channel assigned by the Federal Communications Commission.
explanation: A ship should call another vessel on 2182 kHz or Channel 16 by default, unless it's known the other vessel also monitors a shared working frequency simultaneously.

question: What is the MF radiotelephony calling and Distress frequency?
choices: Ch-06 VHF.
Ch-22 VHF.
explanation: 2182 kHz is the internationally designated MF radiotelephone calling and distress frequency - the MF counterpart to VHF Channel 16.
choice_notes: 2670 kHz: US Coast Guard working frequency (broadcasts).
Ch-06: VHF intership safety channel.
Ch-22: VHF (22A is the Coast Guard liaison channel).

question: For general communications purposes, paired frequencies are:
choices: Normally used with private coast stations.
Normally used between ship stations.
Normally used between private coast and ship stations.
Normally used with public coast stations.
explanation: Paired (duplex) frequencies - one for ship transmit, one for receive - are typically how vessels work public coast stations, unlike simplex intership channels.

question: What emission must be used when operating on the MF distress and calling voice frequency?
choices: J3E – Single sideband telephony.
A1A – On-off keying without modulation by an audio frequency.
F3E – Frequency modulation telephony.
A3E – Amplitude modulation telephony, double sideband.
explanation: The MF distress and calling frequency must be worked using J3E (single-sideband voice), the standard emission for that service.
choice_notes: A1A is Morse on-off keying (CW).
F3E is FM voice, used on VHF.
A3E is double-sideband AM, used by aviation, not marine MF.

question: Which of the following defines high frequency “ITU Channel 1212”?
choices: Ch-12 in the 16 MHz band.
Ch-1216 in the MF band.
The 12th channel in the 12 MHz band.
This would indicate the 1st channel in the 12 MHz band.
explanation: ITU HF channel numbering follows this pattern: the leading digits name the band (12 MHz) and the trailing digits identify the channel within it (the 12th channel).
choice_notes: The first digits give the band: 12xx is the 12 MHz band, not 16.
There's no 4-digit MF channel 1216.
The last two digits (12) give the channel number, so it isn't channel 1.

question: For general communications purposes, simplex frequencies are:
choices: Normally used between ship stations and private coast stations.
Normally used with public coast stations.
Normally used between ship stations.
Both a) and c) are correct.
explanation: Both listed uses of simplex frequencies are correct, as opposed to the paired/duplex frequencies typically used when working a coast station.

question: What is the proper procedure for testing a radiotelephone installation?
choices: A dummy antenna must be used to insure the test will not interfere with ongoing communications.
Transmit the station’s call sign, followed by the word “test” on the frequency being used for the test.
Permission for the voice test must be requested and received from the nearest public coast station.
Short tests must be confined to a single frequency and must never be conducted in port.
explanation: The standard test procedure is to transmit your call sign followed by the word 'test' on the actual frequency being tested, so other listeners know it's not a real call.

question: When testing is conducted on 2182 kHz or Ch-16, testing should not continue for more than ______ in any 5-minute period.
choices: 2 minutes.
1 minute.
30 seconds.
10 seconds.
explanation: To keep the calling/distress channels clear, test transmissions on 2182 kHz or Channel 16 are capped at 10 seconds within any 5-minute period.

question: Under GMDSS, a compulsory VHF-DSC radiotelephone installation must be tested at what minimum intervals at sea?
choices: Daily.
Annually, by a representative of the FCC.
Weekly.
Monthly.
explanation: GMDSS requires a compulsory VHF-DSC installation to be function-tested at least once per day while at sea.

question: The best way to test the MF-HF NBDP system is?
choices: Make a radiotelephone call to a coast station.
Initiate an ARQ call to demonstrate that the transmitter and antenna are working.
Initiate an FEC call to demonstrate that the transmitter and antenna are working.
Initiate an ARQ call to a Coast Station and wait for the automatic exchange of answerbacks.
explanation: Initiating an ARQ call to a coast station confirms the NBDP (telex) system end to end, because the automatic answerback exchange proves both transmit and receive are working.

question: The best way to test the Inmarsat-C terminal is?
choices: Compose and send a brief message to your own Inmarsat-C terminal.
Send a message to a shore terminal and wait for confirmation.
Send a message to another ship terminal.
If the “Send” light flashes, proper operation has been confirmed.
explanation: Sending a brief test message to your own Inmarsat-C terminal confirms the whole message path - composing, transmitting, and receiving - is working correctly.

question: When may you test a radiotelephone transmitter on the air?
choices: Between midnight and 6:00 AM local time.
Only when authorized by the Commission.
At any time (except during silent periods) as necessary to assure proper operation.
After reducing transmitter power to 1 watt.
explanation: On-air testing is allowed whenever needed to verify proper operation, except during the mandatory silent periods, when the channel must stay clear for weak distress signals.

question: Under normal circumstances, what do you do if the transmitter aboard your ship is operating off- frequency, overmodulating or distorting?
choices: Reduce to low power.
Reduce audio volume level.
Stop transmitting.
Make a notation in station operating log.
explanation: A malfunctioning transmitter - off-frequency, overmodulating, or distorting - must be taken off the air immediately to avoid interference and preserve clear communications.

question: Which would be an indication of proper operation of a SSB transmitter rated at 60 watt PEP output?
choices: In SSB (J3E) voice mode, with the transmitter keyed but without speaking into the microphone, power output is indicated.
In SITOR communications, the power meter can be seen fluctuating regularly from zero to the 60 watt relative output reading.
In SSB (J3E) mode, speaking into the microphone causes power meter to fluctuate slightly around the 60 watt reading.
A steady indication of transmitted energy on an RF Power meter with no fluctuations when speaking into the microphone.
explanation: In SITOR and similar keyed data modes, the power meter naturally swings between zero and the rated PEP output as the signal keys on and off; that regular fluctuation is the sign of correct operation.

question: If a ship radio transmitter signal becomes distorted:
choices: Reduce transmitter power.
Use minimum modulation.
Cease operations.
Reduce audio amplitude.
explanation: A distorted transmitter signal means operations must cease, rather than continuing to transmit a degraded, potentially unreadable signal.

question: What would be an indication of a malfunction on a GMDSS station with a 24 VDC battery system?
choices: A constant 30 volt reading on the GMDSS console voltmeter.
After testing the station on battery power, the ammeter reading indicates a high rate of charge that then declines.
After testing the station on battery power, a voltmeter reading of 30 volts for brief period followed by a steady 26 volt reading.
None of the above.
explanation: A 24 VDC GMDSS battery system should read close to its nominal voltage; a constant 30-volt reading points to a charging-system malfunction (overcharging).

question: Your antenna tuner becomes totally inoperative. What would you do to obtain operation on both the 8 MHz and 22 MHz frequency bands?
choices: Without an operating antenna tuner, transmission is impossible.
It is impossible to obtain operation on 2 different HF bands, without an operating antenna tuner.
Bypass the antenna tuner and shorten the whip to 15 ft.
Bypass the antenna tuner. Use a straight whip or wire antenna approximately 30 ft long.
explanation: With the antenna tuner dead, a roughly 30-foot straight whip or wire antenna can still work reasonably well across both the 8 MHz and 22 MHz bands without a matching network.

question: Which of the following conditions would be a symptom of malfunction in a 2182 kHz radiotelephone system that must be reported to the Master, then logged appropriately.
choices: Much higher noise level observed during daytime operation.
No indication of power output when speaking into the microphone.
When testing a radiotelephone alarm on 2182 kHz into an artificial antenna, the Distress frequency watch receiver becomes unmuted, an improper testing procedure.
Failure to contact a shore station 600 nautical miles distant during daytime operation.
explanation: No indication of power output while speaking into the microphone is a clear symptom that the 2182 kHz radiotelephone isn't transmitting properly, and it must be reported and logged.

question: What are the antenna requirements of a VHF telephony coast, maritime utility or ship station?
choices: The shore or on-board antenna must be vertically polarized.
The antenna array must be type-accepted for 30-200 MHz operation by the FCC.
The horizontally-polarized antenna must be positioned so as not to cause excessive interference to other stations.
The antenna must be capable of being energized by an output in excess of 100 watts.
explanation: VHF maritime antennas, shore and shipboard alike, must be vertically polarized to match standard VHF marine radio practice.

question: What is the antenna requirement of a radiotelephone installation aboard a passenger vessel?
choices: The antenna must be located a minimum of 15 meters from the radiotelegraph antenna.
The antenna must be vertically polarized and as non-directional and efficient as is practicable for the transmission and reception of ground waves over seawater.
An emergency reserve antenna system must be provided for communications on 156.800 MHz.
All antennas must be tested and the operational results logged at least once during each voyage.
explanation: A passenger vessel's radiotelephone antenna must be vertically polarized and radiate efficient, non-directional ground waves over seawater, matching how VHF marine propagation works.

question: What is the most common type of antenna for GMDSS VHF?
choices: Horizontally polarized circular antenna.
Long wire antenna.
Both of the above.
None of the above.
explanation: None of the specific antenna types listed is the standard GMDSS VHF answer - GMDSS commonly uses an ordinary vertical whip, which wasn't among the given choices.
choice_notes: Marine VHF is vertically polarized. A horizontal antenna would lose a lot of signal.
Long wires are used on MF/HF, not VHF. (The usual VHF antenna is a vertical whip.)

question: What is the purpose of the antenna tuner?
choices: It alters the electrical characteristics of the antenna to match the frequency in use.
It physically alters the length of the antenna to match the frequency in use.
It makes the antenna look like a half-wave antenna at the frequency in use.
None of the above.
explanation: An antenna tuner electrically adjusts the antenna's characteristics so it presents a good match at whatever frequency is currently in use.

question: What advantage does a vertical whip have over a long wire?
choices: It radiates more signal fore and aft.
It radiates equally well in all directions.
It radiates a strong signal vertically.
None of the above.
explanation: A vertical whip's omnidirectional horizontal pattern radiates equally in every direction, while a long wire tends to favor certain directions.

question: A vertical whip antenna has a radiation pattern best described by?
choices: A figure eight.
A cardioid.
A circle.
An ellipse.
explanation: A vertical whip's horizontal radiation pattern is essentially a circle - roughly equal signal strength in every compass direction.
choice_notes: Figure eight: a dipole viewed from above, or two antennas in phase. Two strong lobes, two nulls.
Cardioid: a heart shape (e.g. loop + sense antenna, two phased verticals). One null.
Ellipse: a slightly directional antenna (stronger in two directions, no deep nulls).

question: For a small passenger vessel inspection, reserve power batteries must be tested:
choices: At intervals not exceeding every 3 months.
At intervals not exceeding every 6 months
Before any new voyage
At intervals not exceeding 12 months, or during the inspection.
explanation: Reserve power batteries on small passenger vessels must be tested at intervals no longer than 12 months, or whenever the vessel is inspected.

question: What are the characteristics of the Reserve Source of Energy under GMDSS?
choices: Supplies independent HF and MF installations at the same time.
Cannot be independent of the propelling power of the ship.
Must be independent of the ship’s electrical system when the RSE is needed to supply power to the GMDSS equipment.
Must be incorporated into the ship’s electrical system.
explanation: The Reserve Source of Energy has to work independently of the ship's main electrical system, since it exists precisely to supply power when that system has failed.

question: Which of the following terms is defined as a back-up power source that provides power to radio installations for the purpose of conducting Distress and Safety communications when the vessel’s main and emergency generators cannot?
choices: Emergency Diesel Generator.
Reserve Source of Energy.
Reserve Source of Diesel Power.
Emergency Back-up Generator.
explanation: This is the definition of the Reserve Source of Energy: backup power dedicated to radio distress and safety communications when the ship's main and emergency generators can't supply it.
choice_notes: The emergency diesel generator is the ship's emergency power source, which the RSE must back up.
Invented term.
Invented term.

question: In the event of failure of the main and emergency sources of electrical power, what is the term for the source required to supply the GMDSS console with power for conducting distress and other radio communications?
choices: Emergency power.
Ship’s emergency diesel generator.
Reserve source of energy.
Ship’s standby generator
explanation: When both main and emergency power fail, the Reserve Source of Energy is the required backup that keeps the GMDSS console operating for distress traffic.

question: What is the requirement for emergency and reserve power in GMDSS radio installations?
choices: An emergency power source for radio communications is not required if a vessel has proper reserve power (batteries).
A reserve power source is not required for radio communications.
Only one of the above is required if a vessel is equipped with a second 406 EPIRB as a backup means of sending a distress alert.
All newly constructed ships under GMDSS must have both emergency and reserve power sources for radio communications.
explanation: GMDSS requires newly constructed vessels to carry both an emergency power source and a separate reserve power source for radio communications.

question: What is the meaning of “Reserve Source of Energy”?
choices: The supply of electrical energy sufficient to operate the radio installations for the purpose of conducting Distress and Safety communications in the event of failure of the ship’s main and emergency sources of electrical power.
High caloric value items for lifeboat, per SOLAS regulations.
Diesel fuel stored for the purpose of operating the powered survival craft for a period equal to or exceeding the U.S.C.G. and SOLAS requirements.
None of these.
explanation: This restates the formal definition: enough stored electrical energy to run distress and safety radio communications if the ship's main and emergency power sources both fail.

question: What is an EPIRB?
choices: A battery-operated emergency position-indicating radio beacon that floats free of a sinking ship.
An alerting device notifying mariners of imminent danger.
A satellite-based maritime distress and safety alerting system.
A high-efficiency audio amplifier.
explanation: An EPIRB is a self-contained, battery-powered beacon designed to float free automatically as a ship sinks and begin transmitting a distress signal on its own.

question: When are EPIRB batteries changed?
choices: After emergency use; after battery life expires.
After emergency use or within the month and year replacement date printed on the EPIRB.
After emergency use; every 12 months when not used.
Whenever voltage drops to less than 20% of full charge.
explanation: EPIRB batteries must be replaced after the unit has been used in an actual emergency, or by the replacement date printed on it, whichever comes first.

question: If a ship sinks, what device is designed to float free of the mother ship, is turned on automatically and transmits a distress signal?
choices: An emergency position indicating radio beacon.
EPIRB on 2182 kHz and 405.025 kHz.
Bridge-to-bridge transmitter on 2182 kHz.
Auto alarm keyer on any frequency.
explanation: This describes the EPIRB's core function: automatic float-free release from a sinking ship, automatic activation, and automatic distress transmission, with no crew action required.
choice_notes: EPIRBs transmit on 406 MHz (with 121.5 MHz homing), not 2182 kHz or 405.025 kHz.
Bridge-to-bridge is VHF Ch-13 voice and doesn't float free.
The auto alarm keyer generated the old two-tone alarm signal on 2182 kHz.

question: How do you cancel a false EPIRB distress alert?
choices: Transmit a DSC distress alert cancellation.
Transmit a broadcast message to “all stations” canceling the distress message.
Notify the Coast Guard or rescue coordination center at once.
Make a radiotelephony “distress cancellation” transmission on 2182 kHz.
explanation: A false EPIRB activation must be reported right away to the Coast Guard or a rescue coordination center, so search and rescue resources aren't wasted responding to it.

question: What is the COSPAS-SARSAT system?
choices: A global satellite communications system for users in the maritime, land and aeronautical mobile services.
An international satellite-based search and rescue system.
A broadband military satellite communications network.
A Wide Area Geostationary Satellite program (WAGS).
explanation: COSPAS-SARSAT is the international satellite system that detects and locates EPIRB, ELT, and PLB distress beacons worldwide.
choice_notes: That describes Inmarsat.
A military broadband satellite network isn't COSPAS-SARSAT.
Invented program.

question: What is an advantage of a 406 MHz satellite EPIRB?
choices: It is compatible with the COSPAS-SARSAT Satellites and Global Maritime Distress Safety System (GMDSS) regulations.
Provides a fast, accurate method for the Coast Guard to locating and rescuing persons in distress.
Includes a digitally encoded message containing the ship’s identity and nationality.
All of the above.
explanation: All the listed advantages of a 406 MHz satellite EPIRB - better position accuracy, unique vessel identification, and faster detection - apply together compared to older 121.5 MHz-only beacons.

question: In which frequency band does a search and rescue transponder operate?
choices: 3 GHz.
S-band.
406 MHz.
9 GHz.
explanation: A Search and Rescue Transponder operates in the 9 GHz (X-band) radar frequency range, matching standard shipboard navigational radar.
choice_notes: 3 GHz is S-band RADAR, which can't trigger a SART.
S-band (3 GHz) RADARs don't interrogate SARTs.
406 MHz is the satellite EPIRB frequency.

question: How should the signal from a Search And Rescue Radar Transponder appear on a RADAR display?
choices: A series of dashes.
A series of spirals all originating from the range and bearing of the SART.
A series of 12 equally spaced dots.
A series of twenty dashes.
explanation: A responding SART produces a distinctive line of about 12 equally spaced dots stretching outward from the survivor's position on the interrogating radar's display.

question: What is the purpose of the SART’s audible tone alarm?
choices: It informs survivors that assistance may be nearby.
It informs survivors when the battery’s charge condition has weakened.
It informs survivors when the SART switches to the “standby” mode.
It informs survivors that a nearby vessel is signaling on DSC.
explanation: The SART's audible alarm activates when it is being interrogated by a radar, letting survivors know a ship or aircraft with radar is within range.

question: Which statement is true regarding the SART?
choices: This is a performance monitor attached to at least one S-band navigational RADAR system.
This is a 9 GHz transponder capable of being received by another vessel’s S-band navigational RADAR system.
This is a performance monitor attached to at least one X-band navigational RADAR system.
This is a 9 GHz transponder capable of being received by vessel’s X-band navigational RADAR system.
explanation: This restates the SART's basic operating principle: it responds to, and is visible on, a vessel's standard 9 GHz (X-band) navigational radar.
choice_notes: A performance monitor is an echo-box style test device, not a SART.
A 9 GHz SART can't be seen on S-band (3 GHz) RADAR.
A performance monitor is a test device, not a SART.

question: At what point does a SART begin transmitting?
choices: It immediately begins radiating when placed in the “on” position.
It must be manually activated.
If it has been placed in the “on” position, it will respond when it has been interrogated by a 9-GHz RADAR signal.
If it has been placed in the “on” position, it will begin transmitting immediately upon detecting that it is in water.
explanation: A SART switched to the 'on' position stays dormant until it detects an interrogating 9 GHz radar pulse, at which point it begins transmitting its response.

question: How can a SART’s effective range be maximized?
choices: The SART should be placed in water immediately upon activation.
The SART should be held as high as possible.
Switch the SART into the “high” power position.
If possible, the SART should be mounted horizontally so that its signal matches that of the searching RADAR signal.
explanation: Since the SART and the interrogating radar both operate line-of-sight at 9 GHz, holding the SART as high as possible significantly extends its detection range.

question: Which statement is NOT true regarding the requirements of survival craft portable two-way VHF radiotelephone equipment?
choices: Watertight to a depth of 1 meter for 5 minutes.
Effective radiated power should be a minimum of 0.25 watts.
Operates simplex on Ch-70 and at least one other channel.
The antenna is fixed and non-removable.
explanation: This is the false statement: survival craft VHF sets are two-way voice radios, not DSC devices confined to Channel 70 - that's what distinguishes this incorrect description from the actual requirement.

question: Which statement is NOT true regarding the requirements of survival craft portable two-way VHF radiotelephone equipment?
choices: Operation on Ch-13.
Effective radiated power should be a minimum of 0.25 Watts.
Simplex voice communications only.
Operation on Ch-16.
explanation: This is the false statement: survival-craft portable VHF sets aren't required to operate on Channel 13 (bridge-to-bridge) - their required channels are Channel 16 and designated on-scene/SAR channels.

question: With what other stations may portable survival craft transceivers communicate?
choices: Communication is permitted between survival craft.
Communication is permitted between survival craft and ship.
Communication is permitted between survival craft and rescue unit.
All of the above.
explanation: A survival craft portable transceiver is built to communicate with all of these: other survival craft, nearby ships, and search-and-rescue aircraft.

question: Equipment for radiotelephony use in survival craft stations under GMDSS must have what capability?
choices: Operation on Ch-16.
Operation on 457.525 MHz.
Operation on 121.5 MHz.
Any one of these.
explanation: GMDSS survival craft radiotelephone equipment must be able to operate on Channel 16, the universal distress and calling channel.
choice_notes: 457.525 MHz is a UHF on-board (handheld) communication frequency.
121.5 MHz is aeronautical emergency/homing.
Only Ch-16 is mandatory.

question: Equipment for radiotelephony use in survival craft stations under GMDSS must have what characteristic(s)?
choices: Operation on Ch-16.
Watertight.
Permanently-affixed antenna.
All of these.
explanation: Survival craft radio equipment must meet all of the listed characteristics together - since it may need to be used by anyone in an emergency, it has to be rugged, buoyant, and simple to operate.

question: What is the minimum power of the SCT
choices: Five watts.
One watt.
¼ watt.
None of the above.
explanation: A survival craft transceiver's minimum required output is 1 watt, enough for short-range communication with nearby rescuers.

question: NAVTEX broadcasts are sent:
choices: Immediately following traffic lists.
In categories of messages indicated by a single letter or identifier.
On request of maritime mobile stations.
Regularly, after the radiotelephone silent periods.
explanation: Each NAVTEX message carries a single-letter subject indicator (for example, 'A' for navigational warnings), letting receivers sort and filter message categories.

question: MSI can be obtained by one (or more) of the following:
choices: NAVTEX.
SafetyNET.
HF NBDP.
All of the above.
explanation: Maritime Safety Information can come from any combination of the listed sources - NAVTEX, Inmarsat SafetyNET, and other designated broadcast services - together.

question: Which of the following is the primary frequency that is used exclusively for NAVTEX broadcasts internationally?
choices: 518 kHz.
VHF channel 16 when the vessel is sailing in Sea Area A1, and 2187.5 kHz when in Sea Area A2.
explanation: 518 kHz (in English) is the internationally designated primary frequency for NAVTEX broadcasts worldwide.
choice_notes: 2187.5 kHz: MF DSC distress alerting.
4209.5 kHz: HF NAVTEX-type MSI frequency, a secondary frequency.
Ch-16 and 2187.5 kHz are voice/DSC distress channels, not NAVTEX.

question: What means are used to prevent the reception of unwanted broadcasts by vessels utilizing the NAVTEX system?
choices: Operating the receiver only during daytime hours.
Coordinating reception with published broadcast schedules.
Programming the receiver to reject unwanted broadcasts.
Automatic receiver de-sensitization during night hours.
explanation: NAVTEX receivers can be programmed to filter out message categories or originating stations the operator doesn't need, screening out unwanted broadcasts.

question: When do NAVTEX broadcasts typically achieve maximum transmitting range?
choices: Local noontime.
Middle of the night.
Sunset.
Post sunrise.
explanation: Like other MF signals, NAVTEX propagation improves at night due to reduced ionospheric absorption, giving its maximum range around the middle of the night.

question: What is the transmitting range of most NAVTEX stations?
choices: Typically 50-100 nautical miles (90-180 km) from shore.
Typically upwards of 1000 nautical miles (1800 km) during the daytime.
Typically 200-400 nautical miles (360-720 km).
It is limited to line-of-sight or about 30 nautical miles (54 km).
explanation: A typical NAVTEX transmitting station reaches roughly 200-400 nautical miles (about 360-720 km) under normal propagation conditions.
